One-sentence judgment: carpentry is not 'nailing boards together' — it is measuring and laying out lumber and similar materials to drawings and specifications, cutting and shaping them, and installing them into usable building structures and fixtures: wood framing (partitions, joists, studs, and rafters), concrete forms, wooden stairs, door and window frames, and hardwood floors, and possibly cabinets, exterior siding, drywall, and insulation, checking plumb and level with a level and plumb bob, and finally leaving process records as reviewable evidence. O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), the page is labeled Bright Outlook, the interest code is RC (realistic, conventional), and the page also lists 34 registered apprenticeship occupation titles. The core boundary is: carpentry is usually not a uniformly licensed occupation, but work at height, scaffolding, temporary electrical power and machinery, structural alteration and demolition, and wood dust and chemical protection requirements come from workplace safety regulations, job training, and institutional authorization; structural alteration plans, load-bearing and demolition decisions, and on-site stop-work authority must be verified separately by jurisdiction and institutional policy.

Signals to keep exploring: you can read drawings and specifications and turn them into dimensions and layout, you are willing to work in an environment of continuous standing and frequent bending, crouching, and climbing (the O*NET work context shows 70% standing continuously or almost continuously, 59% continuously using hands to handle and control objects and tools, 59% working under noise every day, 52% exposed to hazardous equipment every day, 54% working outdoors in all weather conditions every day, and 50% considering the consequences of error extremely serious), you can accept wood dust and noise and consistently wear protective equipment (95% wearing common protective or safety equipment every day), you are willing to self-check dimensions, plumb, and level after each step and write the records clearly, and you stop and report first rather than forcing the work when drawings do not match the site, materials are substandard, or working conditions are unsafe.

Conditions for pausing large investments first: you have not yet completed a full closed-loop exercise from reading drawings and laying out through material selection and ordering, cutting and shaping, installation and fastening, dimensional verification, and handover records; or you are unwilling to follow work-at-height and machinery protection and dust and noise control requirements, unwilling to stop and report per procedure, or unwilling to stand for long periods under noise and dust and weather conditions; also, having done small woodwork at home must not be treated as proof that you already have structural installation, formwork, scaffolding work, and on-site safety judgment ability.

Education, qualification, and authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), and the education survey shows 52% of respondents saying a high school diploma or equivalent is needed, 21% a postsecondary certificate, and 18% that less than a high school diploma is sufficient; this occupation's page lists 26 certifications (including the National Center for Construction Education and Research NCCER Commercial Carpenter and Carpentry, the Door and Hardware Institute Door + Hardware Consultant, and the National Wood Flooring Association Certified Installer and Sand & Finisher), and lists 34 occupation titles approved by the U.S. Department of Labor for registered apprenticeship. In the United States, carpentry is usually not a uniformly licensed occupation, but some states and jurisdictions have separate registration or licensing requirements for contracting and specialty work; in mainland China, work at height, scaffolding, temporary electrical power, lifting, and machinery involve separate workplace safety and special operation provisions. Education and training, industry certification, statutory work qualifications, position hiring and authorization, and structural alteration and stop-work decision authority are five different things.

One sentence: this is a position that turns 'whether this structure and woodwork have been built correctly to the drawings, solidly, and safely' into reviewable evidence, with outputs being layout and dimensional records, material selection and cutting lists, installation and fastening records, plumb and level verification records, progress and cost estimate records, and defect and rectification and handover records; it is not a structural design or approval role, nor does it replace the decisions made by registered designers, structural engineers, safety managers, and supervisors on structural plans, load-bearing alterations, and stop-work and resume-work. Neither the U.S. nor the mainland China wage figure is fixed on this route, and only the framing and lookup entries are registered in the corresponding sections.

The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, reading drawings, laying out, and selecting materials (studying drawings and specifications, measuring and laying out on site, selecting and ordering lumber and materials, and marking and cutting to size); second, installation and construction (setting up scaffolding and temporary supports, installing structural members and framing, installing doors and windows and floors and trim and hardware, anchoring and fastening, and protecting finished work and cleaning the site); third, inspection and handover (checking plumb and level with a level and plumb bob, inspecting for damage and defects, keeping work records and submitting written progress reports, preparing cost estimates, and rectifying and handing over). All three share the same chain centered on dimensional accuracy, solid assembly, and work safety.
Reading drawings, laying out, and selecting materials

Study drawings and sketches and building plans to determine dimensions and materials → measure on site and lay out with chalk lines and marking gauges → select and order lumber and hardware and other materials needed → machine or cut to the marked cutting lines and to the specified dimensions → re-verify dimensions and the plumb and level datum and check the subsequent installation allowance against the specific drawings and process requirements → produce layout and dimensional records and a cutting list
Installation and construction

Set up scaffolding or ladders and place temporary supports → install framing and structural members such as partitions and joists and studs and rafters → install fixtures such as door and window frames and floors and trim and cabinets and hardware → anchor and support with nails and bolts and anchor rods and steel cables → verify plumb and level with a level and plumb bob → clean the site and protect finished work

Check ceilings and floors and walls and exterior siding and woodwork for damage or decay → record defects and decide whether to repair or replace → keep work records and document the work and submit written progress reports → prepare cost estimates and change explanations for the client or employer → rectify and complete handover → escalate matters beyond authority or involving safety hazards to authorized personnel

Carpenters center on the construction, installation, and repair of on-site structures and woodwork; brickmasons and blockmasons specialize in laying masonry and blocks, floor layers (other than carpet, wood floor, and hard tile) specialize in installing resilient and specialty floor materials, tile and stone setters specialize in setting tile and stone, cement masons and concrete finishers specialize in placing and finishing concrete, construction laborers focus on cleanup and carrying and helper work, cabinetmakers and bench carpenters specialize in shop-based wood product fabrication and assembly, and carpenter helpers focus on supervised assistance. Similar names or sharing a construction site do not mean that structural alteration and stop-work and resume-work decision authority, scaffolding and work-at-height qualifications, machinery operating authorization, and installation acceptance signing authority are interchangeable.
Core purpose

To bring structures and woodwork to the dimensional, plumb and level, solidity, and safety requirements of the drawings and standards: reading drawings and laying out keep dimensions verifiable, installation and fastening records keep the process traceable, and verification and handover keep defects from being carried into the next process.
Main subjects and basis

The subjects are materials such as lumber and similar materials and hardware and insulation, as well as on-site structural members and concrete forms and fixtures such as doors and windows and floors and cabinets; the cooperating parties include project managers, designers and technical staff, adjacent trades such as masonry and flooring and concrete, subcontractors (heating, electrical, and other specialty trades), and owners or clients. The basis is the dimensions and specifications in drawings and sketches and building plans, the product instructions and installation requirements for materials and hardware, the plumb and level verification methods and tolerance requirements, the statutory requirements and institutional procedures for workplace safety and work at height and scaffolding and temporary electrical power and lifting and machinery, the occupational health protection requirements for wood dust and noise and chemicals, and the institution's internal work permits and stop-work and resume-work and handover processes.
Core process

Study drawings and specifications, measure and lay out on site, select materials and cut and shape them, set up scaffolding and temporary supports, install structures and fixtures and anchor and fasten them, verify plumb and level with a level and plumb bob, inspect for damage and defects and rectify, document the work and submit progress reports, and prepare cost estimates and complete handover.
Main outputs

Layout and dimensional records, material selection and cutting lists, material and hardware order records, installation and fastening and anchoring records, plumb and level verification records, scaffolding and temporary support erection records, defect and rectification records, work records and written progress reports, cost estimates and change explanations, and handover records.
Accountable parties

Carpenters are responsible for layout, cutting, installation, and self-check records within the authorized scope; design changes, load-bearing judgments, and formal acceptance are borne by the corresponding personnel who are legally qualified and authorized on the project. Scaffolding erection and temporary electrical work additionally require verifying the corresponding trade qualifications, internships, and position authorization; the responsibility of suppliers and inspection stages must be distinguished per the project contract and policy.
Admission and permits

Work qualifications and authorization must be verified item by item by jurisdiction, trade, and equipment; for housing and municipal works in mainland China, whether building electricians and building scaffolders belong to special operations is first verified against the 2026 Special Operations Catalogue, and certificate and practice management is then verified against Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development Order No. 60. First-time certificate holders must complete at least 6 months of supervised internship before formally working and must not work independently (Articles 20—22, effective 2026-06-01). Ordinary woodworking machinery operation, work at height, trade qualifications, position authorization, and formal acceptance duties are verified separately and cannot be merged into one general qualification.
Conclusion boundaries

Dimensional and verification records describe how this structure and woodwork were executed under the given drawings and within the authorized scope; they are not a final determination of structural safety and construction quality, nor do they replace the determinations made by design, supervision, and safety management under standards and policy, and they are updated as design changes and site conditions are supplemented; when citing, state the drawing version, the material batch, and the record period at the same time.

Before starting, verify at least six items: job duties (leaning toward framing and structural installation, doors and windows and floors and finishes, formwork and concrete forming, repair and renovation, or site management and cost estimating), the scope within which independent work is allowed (whether work at height and scaffolding, temporary electrical power, and machinery are involved) and the corresponding training and qualification requirements, whether you need to provide your own tools and protective equipment, the working method (piecework or hourly, whether you travel with projects and live on site), overtime and shift and travel arrangements, and work permits and stop-work and resume-work and assessment methods.
Occupational framing

O*NET-SOC 47-2031.00 (SOC 47-2031) is this page's U.S. occupational framing, Job Zone 1–2, SVP below 6.0; the summary and detail page titles viewed on 2026-10-08 do not show a Bright Outlook occupation marker. Interest code RC, realistic 96, conventional 41; building and carpentry 98, physical and manual labor 88. The industry distribution is 64% construction and 36% other. The occupational scope includes structural framing, concrete forms, and fixtures such as doors and windows and floors. A one-to-one Chinese subcategory has not been established; this does not mean that related carpentry occupations do not exist in China.
Education and training pathways

U.S. BLS lists the typical entry education for carpenters as a high school diploma or equivalent, with no related work experience and apprenticeship as the on-the-job training category. The O*NET Job Zone 1–2 range of a few days to one year applies to the merged occupational group and cannot be treated as the period for a carpenter to complete an apprenticeship or work independently. The O*NET education survey's 52% high school or equivalent, 21% postsecondary certificate, and 18% less than high school are respondents' judgments about the education a position requires, not the educational composition of practitioners. The certification directory and the registered apprenticeship occupation titles on the detail page are learning entries, not Chinese qualifications; the enrollment conditions of specific programs must be verified item by item.
Methods and tools

The O*NET software skills list names 9 categories, and the Hot Technologies page shows 5 items (Microsoft Excel, Microsoft Office software, and Microsoft Word each below 1%, with Intuit QuickBooks and Microsoft Windows given no frequency; the data source is 2025 U.S. job postings from Lightcast), and the list also includes categories such as accounting and cost estimating software, computer-aided design (CAD) drafting software, information retrieval software, and project management and estimating software. On-site methods and tools center on hand tools (rules and marking gauges, levels and plumb bobs, saws and chisels and hammers), power and pneumatic tools (electric drills, power saws, nail guns), woodworking machinery, scaffolding and ladders and temporary supports, measuring and layout tools, and personal protective equipment (hard hats, safety glasses, dust masks, hearing protection, and non-slip shoes).
Safety and work permits

The work is mainly physical labor at a construction site. The O*NET work context shows: 95% wearing common protective or safety equipment every day; 94% having face-to-face discussions every day; 84% in continuous contact with others; 70% standing continuously or almost continuously; 67% considering precision or accuracy extremely important; 68% having extremely high responsibility for the health and safety of others; 67% making decisions every day; 59% continuously using hands to handle and control objects and tools; 59% working under distracting or uncomfortable noise every day; 52% exposed to hazardous equipment every day; 54% working outdoors in all weather conditions every day; 44% exposed to contaminants every day; 50% considering the consequences of error extremely serious; 37% working more than 40 hours per week; 27% working at height every day; 34% at risk of minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day; 27% wearing specialized protective or safety equipment every day; 57% reporting that the work is not automated at all. Work must follow workplace safety and institutional safety procedures, and entering work-at-height, scaffolding, temporary electrical, and machinery areas requires complying with on-site work permits and protective requirements.
Training and regulatory requirements

U.S. contracting and specialty qualifications must be checked against the target state's rules, which were not verified state by state this round; U.S. construction carpentry machinery safeguarding is verified against OSHA 1926.304. For housing and municipal works in mainland China, whether building electricians and building scaffolders belong to special operations is first verified against the 2026 Special Operations Catalogue, and certificate and practice management is then verified against Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development Order No. 60. First-time certificate holders must complete at least 6 months of supervised internship before formally working and must not work independently (Articles 20—22, effective 2026-06-01). Ordinary woodworking machinery operation, work at height, trade qualifications, position authorization, and formal acceptance duties are verified separately and cannot be merged into one general qualification.
Pay and hours

U.S. national 2025 wages: annual wages P10/P25/P50/P75/P90 are 40,410/48,510/60,580/76,830/99,910 USD; the corresponding hourly wages are 19.43/23.32/29.12/36.94/48.03 USD. The median is not a starting wage, and the percentiles are not seniority levels or job offers. The NBS 2025 average annual wage of urban unit employees in the construction industry: 92,036 yuan for non-private units and 66,275 yuan for private units (pretax, yuan/year). This is the unit average for all occupations in the industry and serves only as a reference for the employment environment of construction and installation positions; it is not a carpenter's wage or median or starting wage, and it does not cover self-employed individuals or freelancers. Comparing actual opportunities should also verify the pay method, contractual hours, overtime, travel, and tool costs, and the two places' wages cannot be compared by currency conversion.

Carpenters (O*NET-SOC 47-2031.00, Carpenters) build, erect, install, or repair structures and fixtures made of lumber and similar materials to drawings and specifications: concrete forms; building framing (including partitions, joists, studs, and rafters); wooden stairs, door and window frames, and hardwood floors; they may also install cabinets, exterior siding, drywall, and rolled or roll-form insulation; this includes brattice builders who build doors or brattices (ventilation walls and partitions) inside underground passageways. Daily work includes: measuring and marking cutting lines on materials with rules and pencils and chalk lines and marking gauges; following established safety rules and maintaining a safe and clean working environment; machining or cutting materials to specified dimensions with hand tools or machines or power saws; selecting and ordering lumber or other materials needed; installing structures or fixtures such as doors and windows and frames and floors and trim and hardware with hand or power woodworking tools; verifying the plumb and level of structures with a level and plumb bob; arranging for subcontractors to handle specialty work such as heating or electrical wiring; making or repairing cabinets and doors and frames and floors and other wooden fixtures with woodworking machinery and hand or power tools; removing damaged or defective structural components with hand tools and repairing or replacing them; installing rough door and window frames and subflooring and fixtures or temporary supports in structures under construction or repair; erecting scaffolding or ladders for assembling structures above ground level; keeping work records and scheduling work crews; checking structural lumber and supports for decay and replacing them as needed; filling cracks and defects in plaster or drywall with patching plaster and trowels and sanding tools and sanding them; digging or directing the digging of post holes and setting posts to support structures; applying surface finishes to woodwork or wall panels in houses or buildings with paints and hand tools or paneling; laying waterproof paper on subflooring and installing hardwood and parquet or strip flooring by nailing or bonding; checking ceilings and floor tiles and wall materials and exterior siding and glass or woodwork for damage; preparing cost estimates for clients or employers; keeping records and documenting work and submitting written progress reports; drilling holes in lumber or masonry or concrete walls with electric drills; studying specifications in drawings and sketches or building plans to prepare layout and determine required dimensions and materials; assembling and fastening materials with hand tools and wood screws and nails and dowels or adhesives to make frames or supports; doing limited plumbing or welding or concrete mixing work; anchoring and bracing forms and other structures with nails and bolts and anchor rods and steel cables and boards and wedges and lumber; handling or removing hazardous materials; building sleds from logs and lumber to transport camp buildings and machinery in wooded areas; building forms or chutes for pouring concrete; installing shock-absorbing or sound-insulating or decorative paneling on ceilings or walls; and using drones for site surveying and inspecting hard-to-reach parts of structures. It carries responsibility for dimensional accuracy, solid assembly, and on-site work safety, but does not replace the decisions made by registered designers, structural engineers, safety managers, and supervisors on structural plans, load-bearing alterations, stop-work and resume-work, and acceptance.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 47-2031.00 Carpenters, on the page updated in 2026, listed as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), and the titles viewed this time do not show a Bright Outlook occupation marker; the page lists 34 occupation titles approved by the U.S. Department of Labor for registered apprenticeship. The official duties are 'Construct, erect, install, or repair structures and fixtures made of wood and comparable materials, such as concrete forms; building frameworks, including partitions, joists, studding, and rafters; and wood stairways, window and door frames, and hardwood floors. May also install cabinets, siding, drywall, and batt or roll insulation. Includes brattice builders who build doors or brattices (ventilation walls or partitions) in underground passageways.'; the page lists 30 tasks (25 core + 4 supplementary + 1 new), covering measuring and marking cutting lines on materials (76), following established safety rules and maintaining a safe and clean environment (73), machining or cutting materials to specified dimensions (71), selecting and ordering lumber or materials needed (71), installing structures or fixtures such as doors and windows and frames and floors and trim and hardware (69), verifying the plumb and level of structures with a level and plumb bob (68), arranging for subcontractors to handle specialty work such as heating or electrical wiring (66), making or repairing cabinets and doors and frames and floors (66), and core tasks such as removing and replacing damaged components (64), installing rough door and window frames and subflooring and temporary supports (64), erecting scaffolding or ladders (64), keeping work records and scheduling work crews (64), checking structural lumber for decay and replacing it (63), filling cracks in drywall and sanding them (63), and digging post holes and setting posts to support structures (63); the supplementary tasks include handling or removing hazardous materials (60), building sleds from logs for transport (55), building forms or chutes for pouring concrete (54), and installing shock-absorbing or sound-insulating or decorative paneling (46), and the new task is using drones for site surveying and inspecting hard-to-reach parts.

paragraphs: This page compares carpentry with six adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is a better fit for. Adjacent directions are described by their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean that job titles or work qualifications and signing authority are interchangeable.

Evidence note: occupational direction and core outputs are based on O*NET-SOC 47-2031.00 and the official descriptions of adjacent entries (U.S. framing); the adjacent occupations listed by this evidence route are brickmasons and blockmasons, floor layers (other than carpet, wood floor, and hard tile), tile and stone setters, cement masons and concrete finishers, and construction laborers, with cabinetmakers and bench carpenters as a same-chain direction among O*NET related occupations; structural alteration and stop-work and resume-work decision authority, scaffolding and work-at-height qualifications, machinery operating authorization, and installation acceptance signing authority must be verified separately by each jurisdiction and institutional authorization; this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for switching careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between carpentry and adjacent directions; the basis for judgment is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required qualifications, not how similar the job titles sound.

Brickmasons and blockmasons specialize in laying masonry materials and mortar and usually do not carry wood framing and woodwork fixtures; this occupation produces framing and installation and verification of lumber and similar materials.

If you would rather work with masonry and mortar and do quality control of masonry plumb and mortar joints, examine brickmasons and blockmasons first; if you would rather read drawings and lay out and do wood framing installation, examine this occupation first.
Building walls and structures with brick and blocks and stone, with outputs mainly the quality of the masonry and mortar joints and plumb and level.
Brickmasons and blockmasons

Floor layers (other than carpet, wood floor, and hard tile) specialize in resilient sheet goods and specialty floor materials; this occupation's wood floors and subflooring belong to the woodwork installation chain, and the materials and processes and inspection methods of the two differ.

If you would rather specialize in resilient and specialty floor materials, examine floor layers (other than carpet, wood floor, and hard tile) first; if you would rather do wood flooring and subflooring and framing installation, examine this occupation first.
Installing resilient and specialty floor materials, with outputs mainly substrate preparation and floor installation flatness.
Floor layers (other than carpet, wood floor, and hard tile)

Tile and stone setters specialize in bonding tile and stone and joints and waterproofing; this occupation works with lumber and similar materials for framing and fixtures and does not use the tile and stone bonding processes.

If you would rather do tile and stone surfaces and waterproofing, examine tile and stone setters first; if you would rather do wood framing and woodwork installation and verification, examine this occupation first.
Setting tile and stone and doing joints and waterproofing, with outputs mainly surface flatness and bonding and waterproofing.
Tile and stone setters

Cement masons and concrete finishers specialize in placing and vibrating and finishing concrete; this occupation makes and anchors and removes concrete forms, which is the formwork process rather than the concrete forming process.

If you would rather do concrete placement and surface finishing, examine cement masons and concrete finishers first; if you would rather do formwork and wood framing installation, examine this occupation first.
Placing and finishing concrete members and surfaces, with outputs mainly concrete forming and surface quality.
Cement masons and concrete finishers

Construction laborers focus on cleanup and carrying and excavation and other assistance and usually cooperate with each trade under mentoring; this occupation carries reading drawings and laying out and structural installation and verification responsibility, and the authorization and outputs of the two differ.

If you would rather do site preparation and material transport and gradually learn a skilled trade, examine construction laborers first; if you can already carry reading drawings and laying out and installation and verification, examine this occupation first.
Carrying cleanup, transport, excavation, and assistance work, with outputs mainly site preparation and material transport.
Construction laborers

Cabinetmakers and bench carpenters specialize in shop-based wood product machining and assembly and machine tool operation, mainly for furniture and cabinet products; this occupation produces structures and fixtures installed and verified at a construction site.

If you would rather machine and assemble wood products in a shop, examine cabinetmakers and bench carpenters first; if you would rather do installation and verification at a construction site, examine this occupation first.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risks and work responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of any person or institution; specific procedures and handling processes are determined by the applicable jurisdiction and construction organization design and safety management system and equipment and material instructions and institutional work permits.

Direct answer: the main risks include falls from height and scaffolding instability, power tool and woodworking machinery injuries, occupational health exposure to wood dust and noise and chemicals, rework and weak structural installation from layout and dimensional deviations, unauthorized changes when drawings do not match the site, continuing work when materials and working conditions are substandard, and improper handling of site images and owner information; control depends on pre-work risk confirmation and work permits, scaffolding and protective facility acceptance, machinery guarding and inspection, dust and noise control and personal protection, item-by-item self-check and review of dimensions and plumb and level, material acceptance and handling of non-conforming items, and clear stop-work and resume-work and escalation pathways.

Evidence scope: the occupational scenarios are based on O*NET tasks and work context; this round also verified the OSHA construction carpentry tool rule, the carpentry protection guide, hazardous energy control, and the wood dust eTool, as well as China's Order No. 60. Falls from height and instability of scaffolding or temporary supports cause serious injury or death (27% working at height every day; 68% having extremely high responsibility for the health and safety of others; 50% considering the consequences of error extremely serious).

When danger is present, stop your own work first and report.
Working on scaffolding that has not been accepted or where protection is missing in order to meet the schedule, or altering supports and edge protection on your own.

Power tool and woodworking machinery injuries cause cuts and entanglement and projectile injuries (59% working under noise every day; 52% exposed to hazardous equipment every day; 59% continuously using hands to handle and control objects and tools).

Use per the specific equipment instructions and applicable procedures, keep guards in place, and receive training. When an anomaly is found, stop your own use, keep personnel away, and report; isolating all hazardous energy and servicing and restoration are carried out by personnel trained and authorized for that purpose under a written procedure, and a carpenter must not service the equipment alone after merely cutting power. U.S. shop maintenance references 1910.147, and construction carpentry tools are verified separately against 1926.304, and the two are not conflated into the same scope of application.
Removing or bypassing guards, or using temporary wiring instead of compliant power supply and residual current protection.
Carpenters themselves and workplace occupational health management positions

Occupational health exposure to wood dust and noise and adhesive or paint volatiles causes respiratory and hearing and skin damage with long-term exposure (44% exposed to contaminants every day; 59% working under noise every day; 34% at risk of minor cuts and burns every day).

The employer arranges source dust capture, appropriate ventilation, and position protection according to the exposure assessment; a common mask cannot replace the required respiratory protection. Gloves are selected by chemical and specific task, and chemical protective gloves must not be used on rotating woodworking machinery; the OSHA carpentry guide makes clear the entanglement risk. Occupational health examinations are arranged per the applicable rules and exposure conditions.
Cutting and sanding in a confined space without dust capture and ventilation for convenience, or not wearing hearing and respiratory protection for long periods.

Layout and dimensional deviations or weak installation and anchoring cause rework and failure of subsequent processes (67% considering precision or accuracy extremely important; 57% having extremely high responsibility for the work outcomes of others).

Editorial quality verification suggestion: verify layout and cutting dimensions against the approved drawings, and record the measured plumb and level after installation; allowances are determined by the process requirements, and it cannot be uniformly required that all materials have an allowance. When a deviation is found, pause your affected process and report to the reviewer for confirmation of handling.
Cutting directly from experience without re-checking the drawing dimensions, or leaving deviations for subsequent processes to 'make up'.

Continuing work when drawings do not match the site or materials and working conditions are substandard causes structural safety and quality and rework losses (50% considering the consequences of error extremely serious; 68% having extremely high responsibility for the health and safety of others).

Editorial verification suggestion: record drawing and site differences, damp or deformed materials, and unsafe conditions, pause your affected work, and report; material isolation and return or exchange and design changes and resume-work and acceptance are confirmed by the corresponding authorized personnel on the project under the specific procedures, and carpenters are not granted uniform decision authority.
Changing structural member dimensions or connection methods on your own from experience, or forcing work on a work face that lacks the required working conditions.

Improper handling of site images, owner and resident information, commercial drawings, and contract terms causes privacy and trade secret and compliance consequences.

Use drawings and owner information per institutional policy and permissions, provide them only to those with permission, keep a trail, and avoid entering sensitive information into unapproved external tools or public social platforms.

entries.answer: Build, erect, install, or repair structures and fixtures made of lumber and similar materials to drawings and specifications: measuring and marking cutting lines on materials with rules and pencils and chalk lines and marking gauges; following safety rules and maintaining a safe and clean working environment; machining or cutting materials to specified dimensions with hand tools and machines or power saws; selecting and ordering lumber or other materials needed; installing structures or fixtures such as doors and windows and frames and floors and trim and hardware; verifying the plumb and level of structures with a level and plumb bob; arranging for subcontractors to handle specialty work such as heating or electrical wiring; making or repairing cabinets and doors and frames and floors and other wooden fixtures; removing damaged or defective components and repairing or replacing them; erecting scaffolding or ladders; keeping work records and scheduling work crews; checking structural lumber and supports for decay and replacing them as needed; digging or directing the digging of post holes and setting posts to support structures; applying surface finishes to woodwork; laying waterproof paper and installing hardwood or parquet or strip flooring; checking ceilings and walls and woodwork for damage; preparing cost estimates and submitting written progress reports; drilling holes with electric drills; studying drawings and sketches and building plans; assembling and fastening materials to make frames or supports; doing limited plumbing and welding or concrete mixing; anchoring and bracing forms and other structures; handling or removing hazardous materials; building forms or chutes for pouring concrete; installing shock-absorbing or sound-insulating or decorative paneling; and using drones for site surveying and inspecting hard-to-reach parts.

entries.answer: The main risks include falls from height and instability of scaffolding or temporary supports, power tool and woodworking machinery injuries, occupational health exposure to wood dust and noise and adhesive or paint volatiles, rework and weak structural installation from layout and dimensional deviations, unauthorized changes when drawings do not match the site, continuing work when materials and working conditions are substandard, and improper handling of site images and owner information; control depends on pre-work risk confirmation and work permits, scaffolding and protective facility acceptance, machinery guarding and inspection, dust and noise control and personal protection, item-by-item self-check and review of dimensions and plumb and level, material acceptance and handling of non-conforming items, and clear stop-work and resume-work and escalation pathways.

entries.answer: The fit signals are being able to read drawings and turn them into dimensions and layout, being able to work steadily for long periods under noise and dust and weather conditions, and being willing to self-check dimensions and safety per procedure and escalate promptly when problems are found; what matters is whether you have reviewable layout and dimensional records, installation and fastening records, plumb and level verification records, defect and rectification records, and safe operation records, not just some construction site experience or having done small woodwork at home.

entries: Boundary one: this page's identity framing is O*NET-SOC 47-2031.00 (Carpenters); the occupation page lists it as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0) and labels it Bright Outlook; the official duties are to construct, erect, install, or repair structures and fixtures made of lumber and similar materials to drawings and specifications, including concrete forms, building framing, wooden stairs, door and window frames, and hardwood floors; carpentry is usually not a uniformly licensed occupation, and work at height and scaffolding and fall protection, machinery and temporary electrical power, lifting, and structural alteration are required separately under their own rules.

Boundary two: this evidence route records both the U.S. wage (us-salary-static-unavailable) and the mainland China wage (china-salary-exact-unavailable) as documented_unavailable (severity=non_material), so this page transcribes no specific wage or employment or opening figures: for the United States it provides the official entry for querying by region and statistical period, and for mainland China it retains the statistical framing and source and occupational mapping boundary; the two places differ in framing and period and cannot be compared side by side or converted.

Boundary three: mainland China has no separate nationwide occupational wage statistic for this occupation; the related duties may fall within construction carpentry, decoration woodwork, and wood product processing positions, whose employment forms and work permits and job requirements each differ, and this page judges by the position's actual duties and makes clear that the Chinese page language does not constitute an equivalent Chinese occupation or wage mapping.

Boundary four: the editorial exercises and deliverable suggestions are all simulated materials, and readers should not use them for real structural alteration, formwork and scaffolding erection, or on-site work; the exercise results do not constitute work qualifications or contracting qualifications or institutional position authorization.

Boundary five: this page is composed of public materials such as the O*NET occupational summary and detailed profile and industry distribution and technology list and training and education information and certification information and work context and related occupations comparison, the publication information of the Occupational Classification Code of the People's Republic of China (2022 edition), the MOHRSS Enterprise Compensation Survey Information, public information on workplace safety supervision from the State Administration for Market Regulation, and the ILO task exposure study, together with editorial design; the applicable scope and gaps of each material are marked separately.

paragraphs: FermatMind career content editorial team: this round verified nine sections against O*NET occupational data, BLS wages and employment projections, Chinese construction industry unit wages, OSHA carpentry rules, and China's Order No. 60. The applicable scope of each jurisdiction and document is verified separately.

subject.name: Carpenters
subject.summary: This page's entry corresponds to carpenters (O*NET-SOC 47-2031.00, Carpenters): constructing, erecting, installing, or repairing structures and fixtures made of lumber and similar materials to drawings and specifications — concrete forms, building framing (including partitions, joists, studs, and rafters), wooden stairs, door and window frames, and hardwood floors, and possibly cabinets, exterior siding, drywall, and insulation; measuring and laying out with rules and chalk lines and marking gauges, machining materials to specified dimensions with hand and power tools and machines, installing doors and windows and frames and floors and trim and hardware, verifying plumb and level with a level and plumb bob, checking for damage and decay, and documenting progress and cost estimates; work is mainly physical labor at construction sites (70% standing continuously or almost continuously, 59% continuously using hands to handle and control objects and tools, 54% working outdoors in all weather conditions every day, 59% working under noise every day, 50% considering the consequences of error extremely serious), and its duties do not replace the decisions made by registered designers, structural engineers, safety managers, and supervisors on structural plans, load-bearing alterations, and stop-work and resume-work, and this occupation is labeled Bright Outlook on the O*NET page.
